item.title: He Was Deported to a Country He’d Never Heard of. He May Never Go Free.
item.description:
As he stepped out of the American military cargo plane, Roberto Mosquera still couldn’t tell where he was or why he had been taken there. When federal immigration agents forced him onto a secret flight 30 hours earlier, it was a hot July afternoon in Texas. Now, after traveling thousands of miles, he felt a cold winter’s morning in the air.

He was in the kingdom of Eswatini, a tiny, landlocked country in southern Africa that until recently was called Swaziland. Mosquera had never heard of it. He hadn’t set foot outside the United States since he was 12, when he arrived on a fishing boat as part of the 1980 Mariel boatlift from Cuba with his mother, a sister and her infant daughter. As a teenager, he joined a Miami gang, and in his 20s, he took a plea deal after being charged with attempted murder for shooting a rival gangster in the leg. That would have been grounds to deport him had he been from almost any other country. But Cuba wasn’t cooperating with the United States on deportations, so Mosquera was allowed to stay, provided he checked in with the authorities each year. He built a new life for himself, becoming a specialty plumber and a born-again Christian; he married and had four daughters.

Then one day in June of last year, Mosquera, who is 59, went to renew his work permit at an immigration office. The appointment was usually short; Mosquera had borrowed the company truck so that he could head to a job when he was done. But it didn’t turn out that way. An immigration official told him that his time in America was up. With President Trump now back in office, Mosquera knew these were not empty words. But if the United States couldn’t send him to Cuba, where would he go?

He was taken to the Krome Detention Center, a notorious holding facility for deportees in Miami, then to another in El Paso, Texas, where he was confined without being able to contact lawyers for nearly two weeks. Soon agents told him to get ready to move again. Mosquera was surprised when he was loaded onto a small luxury jet — it seemed to him more like something the singer Marc Anthony would rent, he told me. Along with him were four other detainees, from, as he would later learn, Jamaica, Laos, Yemen and Vietnam. They were transferred to a military cargo plane at a U.S. air base in the East African nation Djibouti, and more than a day later, the five men landed in Eswatini.

Before they could make sense of the situation, they were forced inside a metal cage that was fitted onto a transport truck and driven to the Matsapha Correctional Complex, Eswatini’s maximum-security prison. In a post on X, the Department of Homeland Security had called Mosquera and the four other men “depraved monsters” who were “so uniquely barbaric their home countries refuse to take them back.” Now they were met by dozens of guards wielding large sticks.

That was more than a year ago. Mosquera still sits in that same maximum-security prison with nowhere to go. No charges against him. No way to appeal his predicament. No sign that he will ever be freed. Cuba has not signaled any willingness to take him, and Mosquera says he has no desire to go there. Eswatini will not release him from prison, even though he served his time in the United States and committed no crime in Africa.

I first heard about his case through Alma David, an immigration lawyer at Novo Legal Group in the United States, who represents him. When I reached Mosquera on a WhatsApp video call in early June, he had already spent 11 months behind bars. The Eswatini government refused to let me visit him or any of the others detained with him, so WhatsApp video calls were our main means of communication. As we spoke, Mosquera squinted at me; in detention, he had developed glaucoma, and a doctor told Mosquera he had lost half his vision in one eye and 80 percent in the other. He has struggled to receive treatment for the condition.

“Can I ask you a question?” Mosquera asked me. Behind him I could see the green bars of his cell where he spends his nights and the silhouettes of some of the other prisoners.

“Do you think I’ll ever get out of here?”

Mosquera is one of a growing number of people whom the Trump administration has put into a global administrative limbo. For more than a year, it has been offering millions of dollars — often without disclosing the payments — to foreign governments to take immigrants the United States was having trouble deporting to their countries of origin. This includes not only people with criminal pasts like Mosquera but also deportees who were under court protections not to be returned to their homelands because they faced threats there.

The practice of deporting someone to a so-called third country isn’t new, but it used to be rare. In the past, the United States might deport someone to a place deemed safe — Canada, for instance — or to a country where they had dual citizenship. But in 2019, the first Trump administration began sending thousands of foreign nationals, including people from the Caribbean and Central America, to Mexico. In Trump’s second term, the practice has vastly expanded: At least 35 countries have made deals to take deportees, a list that includes nations as far-flung as South Sudan, Ghana, Palau, Uzbekistan and Moldova, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a monitoring group that tracks the agreements.

The deportations bring up serious legal questions that have been the subject of multiple federal lawsuits. The removals — whether they involve immigrants with criminal histories or not — often happen before deportees can argue their cases before a judge. Some of the countries selected by the Trump administration don’t offer the basic legal protections to which the deportees would be entitled in the United States, such as access to a lawyer. And because they are foreign nationals, with no legal status in the countries to which they have been sent, the deportees generally remain under indefinite detention abroad, without charges and with little or no recourse in American courts. In a written statement to The Times, the Department of Homeland Security maintained that anyone who was deported received due process: “These third-country agreements, which ensure due process under the U.S. Constitution, are essential to the safety of our homeland and the American people.”

A number of the countries that have made the deals are unstable or autocratic and usually desperate for American cash. The Central African Republic is in the middle of a civil war. The Democratic Republic of Congo took 15 deportees shortly before the recent Ebola outbreak. Eswatini, which received $5.1 million in its arrangement with the Trump administration, is one of the world’s last absolute monarchies.

The deals first drew widespread attention when the autocratic President Nayib Bukele of El Salvador accepted a $6 million payment in March 2025 to hold some 250 Venezuelan immigrants in CECOT, his Terrorism Confinement Center, a megaprison he had recently built to house as many as 40,000 Salvadoran gang members. The Venezuelans were later flown home, and many claimed that they were abused and tortured by their prison guards while in custody.

The detention archipelago started growing last fall, when the Trump administration began directing flights to Ghana and Cameroon. Human rights lawyers said that this wave of deportees was made up of immigrants seeking asylum who were protected by court orders from being returned to the countries they had fled. Some were also covered under the Convention Against Torture, a United Nations treaty to which the United States is a signatory, which bans the deportation of people to a country where they were tortured or could face torture.

“They have legal protection which means they cannot be deported to their country of origin, and the U.S. is exploiting that protection by deporting them to other countries instead,” says Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, a rights group that has filed multiple lawsuits in the United States and abroad over third-country deportations. “It is then enlisting those countries to detain and deport them back to their country of origin, where they face persecution, torture and worse.” This workaround, known in international law as chain refoulement, is banned under the Convention Against Torture.

But some never get out. They remain in the third countries to which they are sent, stuck in a kind of purgatory — a new class of prisoner created by America’s widening crackdown on immigration.

Human rights lawyers I spoke to have identified at least two dozen cases in which people have been in long-term detention: the 19 men imprisoned in Eswatini and another six or seven in South Sudan. Some were convicted of assault and murder decades ago and had completed their sentences. Some were living in the United States legally; others were not. Many of the cases had additional complicating factors. Mosquera is caught in a diplomatic quagmire that began with Cuba’s 1959 revolution. Others come from countries without a functioning government or with no diplomatic ties to the country where they are being detained. None of the detainees I interviewed had been allowed to collect passports or any other documents that could serve as identification before they were deported.

The situation, in some respects, has come to resemble a more famous case in which the United States sent detainees abroad in haste: the detention center at Guantánamo Bay. In the wake of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, hundreds of foreign nationals were kept out of the reach of American courts, spending years in prison without ever being charged.

Alma David, who now represents some of the other deportees in Eswatini in addition to Mosquera, compared the situation of the Eswatini detainees to a legal black hole. “It’s like you wake up, and you’re in this place, and there’s no way out,” David said. Once Mosquera was flown out of the United States, there were no options for challenging his detention in American courts, so David helped him find a local lawyer in Eswatini. (That lawyer was blocked from seeing Mosquera for nearly a year.) “People are disappearing into this no man’s land,” she said. “They have no connection to their new country, and they also apparently have no legal rights.”

Of the foreign prisons, the one in South Sudan is perhaps the most troubling. As of June, it had been months since anyone, even their lawyers, had heard from the people believed to be in detention there, men born in Laos, Vietnam, Cuba and Myanmar. The only person I found who was allowed to visit the prisoners was an American congressional aide who went last summer to Juba, the South Sudanese capital, to investigate detentions. Even so, the aide said, U.S. Embassy officials declined to accompany her to the prison. Now she is afraid for the fate of the detainees should South Sudan fall into another civil war.

The Eswatini government did not respond to a list of detailed questions I sent to the prime minister’s office about its arrangement with the United States. But my calls with Mosquera, who had obtained a phone with the help of a friendly prison guard, offered a view of a world where medicine was scarce, power outages were commonplace and food was purchased with money sent by relatives via Western Union to the prison warden.

Among those trapped with Mosquera was Kassim Saleh Wasil, arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Detroit more than a year ago. He arrived in the United States from Yemen in 1977 on an immigrant visa and became a permanent resident. He was convicted of second-degree murder in 1999, serving 20 years in prison. ICE said in a statement that he was one of “the many public safety threats and immigration violators that our officers work to take off the streets every day.”

When I met Wasil, who is now 71, over WhatsApp, I saw that he had lost weight in jail and appeared gaunt. “I thought I had paid my debt to society,” he said. He told me he has tried contacting diplomats from Yemen — which is ruled by dueling governments of civilians, soldiers and rebels — but he had not heard back. Wasil, who is Muslim, told me that his worst fear is that he will die forgotten in a Christian country where he will not receive a proper burial.

On another call, I reached Juan Carlos Font Agüero, another Cuban, who is 60 and has been held in Eswatini since last fall. Font told me he was released from a Florida prison in 2022 after serving a 17-year murder sentence, for killing someone during a fight. He showed me paperwork that he submitted during ICE detention, which showed that he had agreed to be deported to Mexico. He was sent to Eswatini instead, a country with no Cuban Embassy.

Font said he was ready to return to Cuba, and one of his daughters, still in Havana, has petitioned the Cuban government to allow his return. But so far there has been only silence. “I was kidnapped, pure and simple,” Font said of his deportation. “The only thing they didn’t do was put a blindfold on my face.”

In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said the administration was “using every tool available to get criminal illegal aliens out of American communities and out of our country. Our message is clear: Criminals are not welcome in the United States.”

Mosquera arrived in America along with thousands of other Cubans, in Key West. His mother, Matilde del Peral, had been a political prisoner in Cuba, locked up for 18 months after she refused to attend meetings of the neighborhood Communist committee. Not long afterward, Fidel Castro, Cuba’s leader, declared that anyone who didn’t support his revolution was free to go, and President Jimmy Carter promised that the United States would welcome the refugees with “an open heart and open arms.” It was the beginning of an exodus of some 125,000 Cubans, including del Peral and all but one of her eight children.

The evacuation, however, was messy. Del Peral and her children initially were housed in a stadium, and like many of the other refugees, they left the matter of obtaining green cards for a later date as they struggled to start from scratch. Mosquera told me that while his mother fed the family and kept a roof over their heads, she didn’t understand that Miami was different from Havana, where the Castro government had all but eliminated petty crime. “Roberto was never a bad boy,” said his sister María Victoria de Ortíz, who lives in Miami. “It was the bad company that changed him, made him take another path.”

When Mosquera was about 14, he told me, another teenager started referring to their clique of friends as the Latin Kings. The name caught on, and Mosquera began to go by the nickname Power. At first, they were mostly playacting, Mosquera said, getting into fistfights and hiding from local beat cops they knew. But things changed when members of the real Latin Kings — a gang that began in the Puerto Rican community in Chicago — started to migrate to Miami. Suddenly, Mosquera found himself in the middle of a turf war, which began with tit-for-tat attacks between rivals before expanding into something much worse.

A raft of stabbings, shootings and car thefts ensued, with Mosquera and his friends often at the center of them. Mosquera told me that in 1988 he was ambushed at a fairground by rival gang members, who knocked his teeth out with a set of brass knuckles. (He still has rows of gold upper and lower teeth that flash as he speaks.) His gang decided to take revenge. One night in Coconut Grove, a neighborhood in Miami, they shot at a 16-year-old rival gangster, who survived the attack but was wounded in his leg.

Mosquera, who told me openly about many crimes he committed during his gang years, insisted he was not there that night. But fearing a life in prison if he stood trial, he took a plea deal for attempted first-degree murder and received a nine-year sentence. By 1996, Mosquera, then 26, had served his time. He thought he had a new life ahead of him, but as an undocumented immigrant, he was rearrested by immigration agents. Mosquera was caught in what is known as administrative detention — which, at the time, allowed immigrants to be held indefinitely before deportation. With Cuba still refusing to take deportees from the United States, Mosquera was held another six years, serving time in various prisons. A 2001 Supreme Court decision banned this practice, requiring the United States to release administrative detainees after six months if they cannot be deported.

It was during that time that the most brutal aspects of the American prison system came into focus for Mosquera. In 1996, he said, he and four other Cubans demanded a meeting with immigration authorities. Instead, he said, the guards assaulted them with pepper spray and tear gas. Later that night, he told me, a guard captain arrived with a group of subordinates, one of them wielding a metal pipe. Mosquera was beaten unconscious. As Mosquera and I talked, he lifted his right thumb, which is crooked. He hasn’t been able to move it since the attack, he said. (Human Rights Watch, which was alerted to the assault, reported that the men did not receive medical care for more than a week after the guards bludgeoned them.)

Mosquera was finally released in 2002 under an agreement that would allow him to remain in the United States and work, while maintaining regular check-ins with immigration authorities. Raised Catholic, he became a born-again Christian in prison. He also left his gang, even though others who tried to do so had been killed in retaliation, and started a family. As he spoke to me on a video call, he tilted his head back to show me the names of his daughters — Destiny, Faith, Monica and Cynthia — tattooed across his neck and chest.

But he still found his way into trouble. Around 2009, after being pulled over by a police officer while riding his motorcycle, he tried to flee, resulting in criminal charges and three years’ jail time. He told me that after his release, he was cited for two parole violations. But as time passed, he began to put all that behind him. In 2014, Mosquera took a temporary job at a Miami plumbing company.

He rose from apprentice to plumber and eventually to foreman; his former boss described him to me as a man who had turned his life around. “He wasn’t just a hard worker; he inspired the guys around him,” he said, speaking on the condition of anonymity because he employs other immigrants who could be targeted by ICE for deportation.

Mosquera had never paid attention to politics. But by 2024, as Donald Trump again set his sights on the White House, Mosquera was undergoing a political awakening. He saw himself as one of the working-class Americans whom Trump — long popular in Miami’s Cuban American community — said he would defend. Mosquera often went to work with a hard hat emblazoned with a bald eagle, his former boss told me. Mosquera’s sister de Ortíz told me she remembered Mosquera practically stumping for Trump. “He would sit on the patio and say, ‘Trump is going to change everything, you’ll see,’” she said. “He even told his daughter to vote for Trump.”

Still, as Mosquera’s annual immigration date approached last summer, de Ortíz had a bad feeling. It was clear to her that the president’s nationalist message offered no exceptions, not even for the many Florida Cubans who supported him in two victories. “I told him, ‘Don’t go.’ And he told me, ‘No, sister, nothing is going to happen.’”

At the maximum-security prison in Eswatini, the deportees were ordered to strip so they could be examined. Mosquera knew similar treatment from his years in American prisons, but this time he was indignant: He had committed no crime, he thought. The guards ordered a 24-hour lockdown for the prisoners. No calls, no lawyers. Their food was a small piece of bread for breakfast and a bare-bones lunch and dinner; a small piece of chicken was served once a week.

After the Eswatini prisoners were barred from calling their families for a month, the warden brought a phone for the prisoners to use. Mosquera called his sister in Miami. “We’d been looking for him everywhere, and then he tells us he’s in Africa,” she said. With the help of his niece, Mosquera made contact with David. “I could see he was somebody who spent enough time in the U.S. criminal justice system to have a concept of what his rights were, and there was a process that had to be followed,” David said. “He was like, You just can’t do this to me.”

One morning, according to Mosquera, an Eswatini general visited the prison and, along with the warden, demanded that the men all sign papers that the government had prepared saying they had declined legal counsel. The prisoners refused. At one point, the guards began to blast Christian music through loudspeakers and eventually demanded that the men, including Wasil, the Yemeni Muslim, stand outside in the yard and pray as the music played.

Mosquera reached a breaking point in October, he said, when a flight carrying 10 deportees arrived. People were coming in faster than they were going, and he had no answers about what would come next. “I said, ‘Lord, what is the way out?’” he told me. Mosquera told the guards he would not eat until he could see a lawyer and was told why he was being held.

At first, the prison guards ignored Mosquera, treating his hunger strike as a joke. At one point, Eswatini officials claimed in a statement that he was on a voluntary religious fast. As the weeks passed, the effects of the hunger strike became agonizing for Mosquera. He recorded his condition in a handwritten diary. “The kidney pains began, my arms and right foot began to fall asleep,” he wrote on Day 22. “In my body I have a headache and am very tired, a lot of dizziness.”

Mosquera sent me photos of his diary, and as I scrolled through the pages, I could see that he had spent much of the hunger strike writing about his 10-year-old daughter, Faith, whom he last saw a week before he was deported. (Mosquera and the girl’s mother are divorced.) “I miss Faith so much. When we would go buy you little clothes, we’d go eat at the mall that you liked so much, we’d go to the movies,” he wrote. “I felt like the happiest father in the world seeing you happy.”

After Mosquera had gone nearly a month without food, his lawyer, David, reached him through one of the prison guards’ phones, urging him to stop the fast. She said he needed to be strong if they were going to fight, Mosquera told me. Mosquera relented; the only other option was to starve himself to death, he said.

After he ended the hunger strike, the guards allowed him to purchase his own cellphone, using money he had been sent by relatives. It was a small victory, but far from the one he sought.

Only two deportees have managed to return to their countries of origin since arriving in Eswatini. One of them, Orville Etoria, the Jamaican man who was on Mosquera’s flight, was repatriated last year. Etoria, who had been a legal resident in the United States since age 12, had his green card revoked by an immigration judge who ordered him deported in 2009, while he was serving a 25-year sentence for a 1996 murder. After his release in 2021, immigration officials instead allowed him to stay in the United States, provided he made regular check-ins. It remains unclear why he was sent to Eswatini; the Jamaican government says it had not blocked his return, as the Trump administration asserted.

When I called him in the town where he had settled, he told me that being deported at age 62 left him feeling disillusioned by the place that once adopted him. “This administration went for people who had changed because they want to prove a point — that you could never change in their mind,” he said.

When I asked Mosquera to imagine some kind of life back in Cuba, what he conjured was grim. “I’m a loudmouth, as you can see when we speak,” he said. “If I was sent to Cuba, probably they’d lock me up too, just like they did to my mother.”

As we continued to send messages week after week, he told me about the end of his marriage, which came about after years of acrimony. His divorce was made official three days before he was deported, but he had always been close to his children, especially Faith. Now he had stopped calling even her. “I need to get the hell out of here,” he texted me one morning. “My life is passing.”

I asked Mosquera why he hadn’t talked to his daughter. He paused for a minute and then started telling me about the day of his ICE arrest. A judge granted him joint custody of Faith, and they were about to spend their first week together, he said. She was home waiting for Mosquera when he was detained. “And now she asks me, ‘When are you coming home?’ It is the greatest pain I ever had — I’ve cried like a child,” he told me. “I, who have been stabbed and shot, I never cried. If I let myself think of her, I will break.”

One day Mosquera mentioned that he had begun a long-distance relationship with a woman. I asked if I could speak to this new girlfriend, and he sent me a South Florida number with the name Ivy Mercado. When I called Mercado, who works for a health care company from her home in Jupiter, Fla., she told me that she met Mosquera in the 1980s when he was dating a friend of hers. They had fallen out of touch, but when word spread that Mosquera had disappeared into ICE custody, she said, “I cried like a baby, and I couldn’t understand why was this affecting me so hard.” A mutual friend sent her Mosquera’s phone number, and they had a long conversation late last year. Mercado called again. She soon realized she was in love.

If there was one thing that seemed to be sustaining Mosquera during his detention, it was his relationship with Mercado. Sometimes Mosquera would talk nostalgically with her about 1980s Miami. Mercado would often tell him about legal research she had done on his case. As we talked, Mercado told me that she was well aware that Mosquera’s imprisonment, which brought them together, is also the thing that keeps them apart. “I tell him: ‘It’s God’s orchestration. You know, we have to believe that,’” she said. “And he’ll say: ‘Well, it brought you to me. It brought us to each other.’”

One morning in July, my phone buzzed. I could see Mosquera had sent me several shaky videos he had just filmed from the prison courtyard. In one, there was a convoy of four vehicles, including what looked like a military truck, entering the grounds. In another, 11 people filed past, some wearing white uniforms. One of them raised his fist in a gesture of resistance. A new group of prisoners had arrived, the third since Mosquera’s flight last year. “No cubanos,” he wrote to me. “One Belize. One Jamaica 🇯🇲 the rest from Africa.”

I called Mosquera, and he began handing the phone to the new arrivals. They looked nervous on the video call. Like Mosquera, they said they had not heard of Eswatini before they arrived. All of them said they had criminal records — some for violent crimes — that had led to their deportations, but they had not expected to be sent to this corner of Africa. Several of them told me they were under protective judicial orders that barred them from being returned to their home countries, where they would be at risk of persecution. They now feared Eswatini would simply forward them to the places they had fled.

One of them, a 64-year-old pastor from Jamaica, named Junior Alves, told me a judge had barred him from being deported to his country because of threats to his family. He said he first came to the United States in 1982. He was arrested on various drug charges when he was a young man, he said, but he had since turned his life around.

Alves handed the phone back to Mosquera. Until now, it had been months since the United States sent new deportees to the prison, but Mosquera was sure there would be more — the guards had been clearing more space, giving everyone new bars of soap.

Now Mosquera had work to do. He needed to show the new arrivals how to get money sent from home. Where they would wash their clothes. What to do when the power went out.

But what everyone really wanted to know was how long Mosquera had been in Eswatini.

“I tell them a year,” he said. “And they get sick to their stomach.”

Nicholas Casey is a staff writer for the magazine based in Madrid.

item.title: This Year’s El Niño Is Huge and Already Changing the World
item.description:
El Niño is the planet’s naturally recurring chaos agent, scrambling weather patterns, spiking global temperatures and typically reaching full strength by December.

But this year’s El Niño, which is expected to be record-breaking, is already strong and having big effects, nudging up global temperatures and causing dry spells and crop failures on multiple continents.

Parts of Panama, normally one of the wettest countries on Earth, haven’t had a major storm since early May. Ethiopia’s fertile highlands are enduring one of their driest summer stretches in four decades. And India had its fifth-driest June since the country’s modern rain records began in 1901.

“This is a good sign that the El Niño response has really kicked in,” said Chris Funk, director of the Climate Hazards Center at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Dr. Funk termed it an “early onset El Niño.”

These on-the-ground consequences reflect the magnitude of the changes in the Pacific Ocean, where El Niños develop when unusually warm waters build up. These episodes occur every two to seven years and have contributed to planetary swings going back millenniums. But this year’s is on track to be the strongest in nearly 80 years of records.

Scientists are debating whether human-caused climate change is tilting the odds toward stronger and more frequent El Niño events. The El Niños of the past few decades have been comparably strong. But the variables that combine to create an El Niño are complex, and some experts argue the recent trend could just be a random signal.

What’s clear is that El Niño’s gyrations are adding to the stronger storms, drier dry spells and fiercer wildfires that global warming is already bringing about. El Niño will magnify those phenomena in some regions and could lift global temperatures to record levels next year, as the heat from the Pacific spreads around the world.

“What we’ll see in 2027 is a sneak peak of what the new normal will be in 2035,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth, a nonprofit research organization. “We’ll see things that have never happened before in our history in terms of temperature, drought conditions, extreme heat.”

El Niño events are measured by looking at sea surface temperatures in a specific rectangular zone of the Pacific Ocean. Temperatures there have soared over the past three months, and forecasts suggest that, by year’s end, they could exceed normal levels by more than they did during the strongest El Niños in modern history, which occurred in 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16.

Between October and December, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says there’s an 81 percent chance that El Niño conditions will be “very strong,” meaning the three-month average temperature in that zone of the Pacific is 2 degrees Celsius, or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, higher than normal. But forecasts show that daily ocean temperatures during that period could spike to more than 3 degrees Celsius above normal.

“Maybe it doesn’t sound that big: three or even four degrees. We see that temperature variation over the course of a day,” said Samantha Stevenson-Karl, an associate professor and climate modeler at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “But the ocean doesn’t change that much. Like, ever.”

The extra heat in the waters of the Pacific affects air temperatures, too. For the first months of the year, 2026 was clearly cooler than 2024, the planet’s hottest year on record. But Dr. Hausfather still gives 2026 a 40 percent chance of being Earth’s warmest year on the books, a sign of how the pendulum could be swinging. According to NOAA, last month tied July 2024 as the world’s warmest July since global record-keeping began in 1850.

El Niño causes big shifts in the winds that blow moist air across the oceans, and the effects on rain-fed agriculture are already emerging in some regions. By the end of the year, El Niño could cause nearly 50 million more people across the globe to experience acute hunger, an increase of roughly a fifth, according to the United Nations World Food Program.

At the western end of the tropical Pacific, El Niño has led to a dry summer in parts of Southeast Asia, delaying the sowing of rice and other crops in Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and the Philippines. In India, monsoon rains have picked up in some regions in recent weeks, though large areas of the country remain in a rainfall deficit.

At the other end of the Pacific, El Niño has delayed planting and disrupted crop growth in Central America. Rainfall in Guatemala was as much as 85 percent below average in July, and the stress on crops has been compounded by well-above-normal temperatures.

In Panama, the dry stretch has raised concerns about operations in the Panama Canal. During the last El Niño, in 2023-24, a severe rain deficit snarled traffic in the waterway, which raises and lowers ships through the locks using water from a rain-fed lake.

As El Niño has gained strength, the Panama Canal Authority has tightened limits on how heavily loaded ships can be while crossing. Officials haven’t ruled out restricting daily transits, according to a statement last week from a spokesman for the canal authority, Octavio Colindres.

It’s hard to predict just how much below normal Central America’s rainfall will be in the coming months, said Steven Paton, who monitors the oceans and atmosphere at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama.

The reason, he said, is that scientists’ computer models are trained on past events. This year’s El Niño is expected to be so much stronger than any episode on record that we can’t be sure how accurately the models will anticipate its effects.

“At the very least, it’s going to be as bad as the worst we’ve seen before, possibly much worse,” Mr. Paton said.

In East Africa, El Niño usually brings heavy rain, and even floods and landslides, from November through January. But when the phenomenon appears earlier in the year, it can suppress rainfall in parts of the region, including western Kenya and Ethiopia.

That’s been the dire reality in recent months, said Chris Shitote, a field scientist based in Nairobi, Kenya, for the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, an agency under the U.S. State Department.

Mr. Shitote and some colleagues recently traveled through Kenya’s western grain-producing counties. The maize harvest was stunningly bad, he said. “It’s something some of us have not seen for the maybe 10 years we’ve been going out.”

Plants that normally grow to be nine feet tall topped out at just five or six feet, Mr. Shitote said. A typical harvest might yield 20 to 30 bags of corn for each acre of field, growers told him. This year, it looks like it could be just one or two bags per acre.

item.title: More Than 40 Dead After a Ferry Capsizes on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba
item.description:
At least 44 people are dead and an unknown number are still missing a day after a crowded ferry overturned in Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba, the country’s president said on Wednesday.

“It is with a heavy heart and profound sadness that I learned of the tragic capsizing,” said Emmerson Mnangagwa, president of Zimbabwe, in a statement on Wednesday about the accident, which occurred on Tuesday and has raised questions about the ferry’s safety and operations.

He thanked private citizens and government security teams, noting that “without their swift response, many more lives would have been lost in the rough and choppy conditions” on the lake that day.

While dozens of people have been rescued — at least 67, the Zimbabwe police said — the search for more missing continued through Wednesday and will resume on Thursday.

Still, just how many passengers may have been on board the ferry when it capsized is unclear, the authorities say. There are indications that the vessel was packed well beyond its designated capacity, the police noted.

The ferry was run by the Rural Infrastructure Development Agency, a quasi-governmental department tasked with the development and maintenance of infrastructure, water supplies, roads services and more. The boat had an official capacity of 90 passengers, excluding crew, but initial indications suggested there were about 120 passengers on the vessel when it overturned, according to the national police.

Based on their investigations, the police suspect the true number could have been even higher, officials said.

The vessel left from the resort town of Kariba and was headed to Chalala, a remote fishing camp on the shores of Lake Kariba, which is the world’s largest man-made lake by volume. According to a declaration of disaster by the president, it capsized after being struck by strong waves while navigating near Long Island, an island about 10 miles from Kariba.

The Department of Civil Protection is coordinating a search and rescue response with the national police’s underwater unit, the Zimbabwe National Army Boat Squadron, local authorities and others. A privately owned helicopter from the Matusadonha Conservation Trust, a national park, has also been deployed to support aerial search efforts, according to the presidential declaration.

Zimbabwe’s public broadcaster said on Wednesday evening that search and rescue operations had stopped for the night and would resume again on Thursday, with divers concerned that there were still people trapped inside the capsized ferry. It said that there are plans to tow the ferry to a nearby island.

“This tragedy has exposed serious deficiencies in our maritime capabilities which we have to address immediately so that our places of recreation do not become death traps to the innocent,” Mr. Mnangagwa said, in an apparent reference to the ferry being overcrowded. And he directed all agencies associated with maritime safety, including specialized units within the security forces, “to take an active interest in ensuring remedial interventions” in light of Tuesday’s accident.

Mr. Mnangagwa called on Zimbabweans to “unite in prayer for the souls of the departed, for the success of the ongoing search operations, speedy recovery of survivors and for comfort and strength for the bereaved families.”

The eclipse began just after 6 p.m. Central European Time (around 12 p.m. Eastern time) in the northernmost part of Russia. The shadow of the moon swooped down to Greenland and Iceland, then farther south across parts of Spain. By 9 p.m., the eclipse ended as the sun set in the Mediterranean.

item.title: Settler Siege of Palestinian Homes Highlights Growing West Bank Chaos
item.description:
Two Palestinian families have been trapped since Sunday inside their homes on a rocky West Bank hillside by a group of violent Israeli settlers, who set up a tent in the front yard of one of the houses. Residents say about 10 to 15 settlers have been attacking them around the clock, throwing stones and an ax.

Early Wednesday morning, after news of the siege began to draw news attention, the Israeli army’s commander for the West Bank, Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, showed up in the village of Qusra and listened as one of the families described how the settlers had been terrorizing them since January. Outside, his soldiers tried to disperse the settlers with tear gas.

Yet, by 10:20 a.m., videos from security cameras show, the soldiers had left. Soon after, residents said, the settlers resumed their attacks.

“We had some hope in the morning when we saw that the army was present,” Aisha Hassan, 35, who was in the meeting with General Bluth, said by telephone, even as she said one of the settlers was throwing stones at her. “But when we saw that the army could not stop the settlers — now, honestly, we are more afraid.”

On Wednesday evening, the army said in response that it was assigning an extra battalion to the West Bank to try to “strengthen order and operational control in the area.”

The army’s initial retreat and broader struggle to contend with settler violence cast a spotlight on the increasingly chaotic situation in the West Bank, where hundreds of Israeli settlers have been terrorizing Palestinians with near-impunity all year.

As of late July, 18 Palestinians have been killed by settlers, one more than in all of 2025, according to U.N. data. Settlers have been boasting on social media of their attacks, posting videos showing mosques that have been torched in Palestinian towns.

At times, soldiers have taken part in the violence, Palestinian and Israeli officials say, reflecting disciplinary problems that the military has acknowledged are an issue.

“It’s a great fiasco,” said Gadi Shamni, a retired two-star general and former head of Israel’s Central Command, whose area of responsibility included the occupied territory. “There’s a loss of control over the West Bank.”

Israel’s right-wing, pro-settler government says that concerns about settler violence are overblown, and officials have repeatedly signaled their support for Israelis accused of attacks. The defense minister, Israel Katz, boasts of having stripped the army of the authority to issue detention orders for settlers — which had been a key tool for restraining Israeli extremist violence. In July, he visited in prison a settler arrested as a key suspect in the sexual assault of a Palestinian man in March and clashed with General Bluth over the suspect’s detention.

In Qusra, located near the city of Nablus in the northern West Bank, the violence has afflicted two families in particular: the Hassans and their neighbors the Abu Ridis.

Louai Abu Ridi, 46, a native of Qusra who immigrated to Ohio in 2003 and is a U.S. citizen in the gas-station business, said he had poured about $1 million into building a house in his birthplace. The settler attacks, beginning in January, started to lay waste to his investment, he said. His brother moved into the house to try to protect it.

Mr. Abu Ridi said he had appealed to the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem for help and was told to report the attacks to the Israeli authorities. An embassy spokesman did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

Ms. Hassan, whose brothers Yusuf and Rizq built two other homes on land owned by their father, said that settlers had broken windows and doors, cut utility lines, destroyed solar panels and stolen the birthday gifts a 2-year-old had received days earlier.

Residents said the settlers appeared to be based in an unfinished home outside Qusra. In March, witnesses said, settlers based in that same home killed another Qusra man, Amir Odeh, and beat and stabbed his father.

Sometimes the settlers have tried to intimidate the families, grazing sheep on their land and destroying their plantings. But the violence has escalated, Ms. Hassan said. Settlers once tried to push the family’s cooking-gas tank into the house through an open window, she said. They’ve fired gunshots and thrown Molotov cocktails at the house, she added.

Efforts by New York Times reporters on Wednesday to reach the scene and speak with the settlers and residents were rendered fruitless by roadblocks guarded by soldiers and settlers.

On Sunday, after the settlers set up camp just outside the Hassans’ homes and erected a tent, the family called the police. When an Israeli soldier showed up, Ms. Hassan said, he ignored the family and instead greeted the settlers warmly. Video recordings show him joining the settlers in prayers.

On Monday night, when Ms. Hassan’s 2-year-old niece, Hoor, spiked a fever and the family called an ambulance, she said, settlers blocked the ambulance and, the driver said, tried to ram it with an all-terrain vehicle. Late Tuesday afternoon, other soldiers made it possible for another ambulance to take the girl to a local clinic, Ms. Hassan recounted.

The military issued a statement on Tuesday acknowledging reports of Israelis seizing Palestinian homes and land in Qusra and expressing “condemnation” for what it called “illegal, reprehensible and unacceptable” actions. On Wednesday, it said that disciplinary action would be taken against the “security personnel involved.”

General Shamni, the retired Central Command chief, said that what had allowed him to keep the Israeli-occupied West Bank relatively calm during his tenure, from 2007 to 2009 — close cooperation with the Israeli police, the Internal Security Agency and the military’s Civil Administration — could no longer be counted on. Pro-settler extremists, like the cabinet ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, wield too much influence over all those agencies, General Shamni said.

Moreover, he added, the military units serving in the West Bank are largely composed of soldiers who grew up in the settlements. “They are the settlers,” he said. “That’s the problem.”

General Shamni said he wished that President Trump would force Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has minimized settler violence, to crack down on it.

General Bluth’s visit to Qusra on Wednesday appeared to signal a new resolve to address the situation, but it evidently alarmed the settlers. The young men who had been attacking the Qusra homes were quickly joined by scores more, who could be seen throwing stones onto the road to make it impassable and then scuffling with soldiers, according to witnesses and video viewed by a reporter.

Soldiers confiscated a tarp and an all-terrain vehicle but ultimately drove off, leaving the settlers behind.

They were still there on Wednesday night.

Gabby Sobelman contributed reporting.

item.title: Arabian Sea Bird and Turtle Habitat Threatened by Oil From Grounded Tanker
item.description:
An oil spill from a Russian shadow fleet tanker that ran aground two months ago has spread its long, black tongue across a remote, ecologically sensitive swath of the Arabian Sea, according to satellite data and statements from Oman’s government.

The spill has encircled the rocky cliffs of an Omani island, Jazirat al Qibliyah, that is home to a range of endangered seabirds, and spread to a 25-mile stretch of beach on the mainland, called Ras Madrakah, Oman’s environmental agency said Wednesday in a statement carried by the state news agency.

A British maritime disaster management company, called Ambrey, has been hired to rescue the tanker and stop the spread of the spill, according to the company. “This is an extremely challenging situation, compounded by adverse weather conditions,” said Ed Wollaston, director of global response at Ambrey.

The spill compounds the environmental consequences of three widening, overlapping conflicts that have made oil and gas infrastructure targets of war in recent months. Russia and Ukraine have attacked each other’s energy facilities. In Yemen, the Houthi militia has attacked oil tankers tied to Saudi Arabia. And the United States and Iran have attacked oil installations and tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

Several oil spills have been detected from satellite images in the strait, including a fairly significant one off Iran’s Kharg island, according to Brian Barnes, a geographer at the University of South Florida. None of them are anywhere near as large as the massive spills of the 1991 Gulf war, when Iraqi forces set ablaze hundreds of oil wells and caused one of the world’s worst environmental catastrophes, which took years to clean up. But swift cleanups are impossible with the ongoing conflict, and even the ecological impacts of the spills are hard to gauge at the moment.

“Satellite observations are great and can tell us a lot,” Mr. Barnes said. “But we don’t have the capacity to go out and see.”

On Tuesday, Iranian state media posted images of oil contamination spreading to Qeshm Island, including an area, known as Shib Deraz, where the rare hawksbill sea turtle nests every spring. Iranian government officials have said nothing about the cause of that spill.

The spill in Omani waters appears to be among the largest of several in the waterways of the Middle East. Estimates vary widely on the scale of the contamination, and what caused it in the first place remains a mystery. All that is certain is that Oman’s government has been forced to respond, because the tanker crashed into the rocky shoals of Qibliyah on a windy day in June.

It seems to have had little to do with Oman, or the conflicts in the region.

The tanker, known as the Caroline Bezengi, is about 900 feet long and capable of carrying nearly a million barrels of oil. It had been used for the last couple of years to ferry Russian crude oil to refineries in Asia, according to TankerTrackers.com, a company that monitors global oil shipping.

In the past, it was flagged under Cameroon. Its managing agent was a firm registered in Cyprus, called Lagosmarine, which was under sanctions by the United States and European Union for helping finance Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Since May, 2023, it had made 12 trips from ports in Russia to ports in India and Pakistan, and once to China, according to logs kept by TankerTrackers.com. In 2025, its crew had complained of not being paid for months, the Seafarers Union of Russia told Russian media outlets.

Its latest journey began on May 13 from the Russian port of Novorossiysk, on the Black Sea, according to TankerTrackers.com. It was headed for Sikka, a port on the western coast of India that serves the world’s largest refinery complex, near Jamnagar.

India, which has not signed on to Western sanctions imposed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, has instead sharply increased its purchase of Russian oil since that war began in 2022.

India’s growing economy needs a lot of oil, and its refineries, including the Jamnagar complex, have made a thriving business from exporting refined products to fuel-hungry countries.

The Caroline Bezengi did not reach India this time.

On June 6, the ship encountered “an incident” outside Oman’s territorial waters, the head of the country’s Environment Authority, Abdullah Bin Ali Al Amri, said in an interview on Oman TV.

Whether the incident was caused by malfunctioning equipment on the ship or by an attack remains unknown. No party has accepted responsibility.

By June 21, according to the Omani government, the ship ran aground on the rocks of the Qibliyah Island. “Reconnaissance measures were taken to inspect the ship’s safety, and indeed, at that time, there was no noticeable oil spill,” Mr. Al Amri said in the television interview.

By late July, there was a noticeable spill. By early August, it had spread.

Oman’s Environment Authority said this week that the slick covers around 390 square kilometers.

Greenpeace said that by Aug. 4 it had covered 600 square kilometers, a fourfold increase in just two days. “The situation surrounding the tanker Caroline Bezengi is yet another alarming example of the serious environmental risks posed by Russia’s so-called shadow fleet,” the organization said in a statement.

John Amos, head of an organization called SkyTruth, which uses satellite imagery to track oil contamination, estimated the coverage area to have grown to roughly 2,200 square kilometers. He said the Omani government’s estimate appears “far too low.”

Mr. Amos said if all of the Caroline Bezengi’s oil leaked, the spill would be comparable to the Exxon Valdez disaster, one of the worst spills in American history that killed hundreds of thousands of seabirds, otters, seals and whales.

Ambrey, the maritime response firm, said in a statement to The New York Times that it was working with the Omani Air Force to stabilize the ship and that ships to help with the salvage operation were en route.

Shadow fleet tankers are often uninsured, and shipowners rarely come forward. Oman is left with the task of monitoring and stanching the damage. The Environment Authority, in its latest statement on Monday, said the slick was advancing quickly in a northeasterly direction.

It said it was trying to protect the most environmentally sensitive areas. “Efforts are being directed towards identifying zones most vulnerable to impact and correlating them with pollution drift trajectories, with particular emphasis on areas of high ecological value and sensitivity,” the ministry said.

Zane Irwin and Ismaeel Naar contributed reporting

item.title: A City Mobilizes Against a Stubborn Health Threat: Mosquitoes
item.description:
It’s been 10 years, but Paulo Gomes still vividly remembers the terror he felt that his wife, Lucirene, would never return from the hospital, that she would die instead of the dengue she contracted from a mosquito bite, her body racked with fever and excruciating pain.

She did come home, after 15 days, and recovered fully after several more months. But the experience forever changed how Mr. Gomes thought about mosquitoes.

Mr. Gomes, now 65, is an eager participant in an aggressive campaign by Belém, the northern Brazilian city where he lives on the edge of a rain forest, to reduce mosquitoes and the health dangers they bring.

Municipal workers have counseled him that mosquitoes breed in standing water and thrive in musty, moist spaces. He fills the swimming pool in the backyard every Friday for his grandchildren who live nearby, but drains it religiously every Sunday after they leave.

He and his wife keep their veranda scrupulously clean and uncluttered, just a tricycle in one corner, a hammock in another — and, since last summer, a plastic bucket that is a centerpiece in Belém’s multipronged strategy against mosquitoes.

The size of a small trash can, it offers just the sort of dark, watery cavity a female mosquito might seek to lay eggs. But it contains larvicide, a chemical that kills young mosquitoes, and when she lands inside she becomes coated with it. When she flies away, she will spread it to other breeding sites, typically within a quarter-mile radius. Last year, Belém distributed 5,000 units in the parts of the city hit hardest by dengue.

At the moment, mosquitoes are a bigger menace in Belém and the rest of Brazil than in the United States or Europe, but the warming planet is expanding their range. Most cases of dengue, malaria and chikungunya in those places were contracted during travel abroad, but locally acquired cases are occurring more frequently. In 2024, the United States recorded nearly 3,800 cases of dengue, more than 100 of them locally acquired. About a third of the patients were hospitalized, and six died.

“The climate crisis is a public health crisis,” Dr. Alexandre Padilha, Brazil’s health minister, said in an interview.

“It’s not a coincidence” that during its Group of 20 presidency, Brazil championed new initiatives to combat climate-driven diseases like dengue, Dr. Padilha said. “We have a lot to learn and also to teach many regions in the U.S.A. about how to face the impact of climate change,” he said.

Forged by bitter experience, Brazil has embraced new techniques to combat mosquitoes. Most of them are environmentally friendly, including building the world’s largest “mosquito factory,” a facility that produces mosquitoes containing Wolbachia, a bacterium that blocks dengue and other viruses. The Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes are then released in communities to breed and pass the bacteria to the next generation.

Tackling mosquitoes requires more than gee-whiz science. Municipal departments will need to beef up their vector control divisions and budgets, doctors must be trained to recognize and treat the diseases, and the general public will need education on protecting itself.

“It’s important for other countries to get ready for the possibility of having more and more cases happening, and train all the layers of the society,” said Luciano Moreira, the chief executive of Wolbito do Brasil, a joint venture between the nonprofit World Mosquito Program and the Brazilian government.

“It’s not just something like the government just goes there and sprays,” he said. “It’s part of a movement.”

Locals like to say Belém has only two seasons — one in which it rains every day, and one when it rains all day.

The city is a gateway to the mighty Amazon, and it is edged by lush, muddy rainforest. Mango trees and their fallen fruit line the streets, luring insects with their sweet sticky scent. Small puddles of water — on the sidewalks, in stacked tires and in trash cans — offer mosquitoes the perfect nurseries to grow millions more of themselves.

For decades, Belém residents have been under attack by Aedes aegypti, the type of mosquito that carries dengue, Zika and chikungunya — so much so that in 2018, a city park installed a large fiberglass statue of the insect. (Aedes aegypti is also found in many parts of the United States, including Florida, Texas and California.)

Climate change has allowed these mosquitoes to multiply faster, intensifying the threats they carry. In 2024, dengue infected more than 10 million people in Brazil and killed more than 6,000. There might have been even more deaths if doctors in Brazil did not know how to recognize and treat the disease promptly, said Moises Silva, a microbiologist at the ⁠Federal University of Pará in Belém.

Brazil’s toll that year was about four times the previous number, and in Belém, it was about seven times higher, flooding the city’s hospitals and forcing a reckoning. City officials adopted myriad methods in response, from increasing common-sense solutions like garbage disposal and treatment of sewage to collaborating with academic scientists like Dr. Silva.

It was Dr. Silva who petitioned the health minister to include Belém in the list of 10 cities that would try out the special larvicide dispensing buckets, and to fund training and equipment for city workers.

Dr. Silva and his colleagues looked at the distribution of dengue cases across the city. They also factored in data from the city’s entomology lab on mosquito larvae and egg traps to gauge the size of the population that season.

Based on those two streams of information, they identified the most vulnerable areas, down to the street level, many of them in low-income neighborhoods and favelas, that would benefit from the units.

Unlike mosquito traps that kill females, the larvicide units, which cost less than $2 each, use the females to spread the chemical to breeding spots that would be hard for humans to find, Dr. Silva said. “We’re using the mosquito against the mosquito,” he said. “That’s the smart thing about the trap.”

The city also trained the workers to educate residents in the low-income areas on ways to keep mosquitoes at bay, to recognize dengue symptoms and to head to the hospital at the signs of severe illness. High fever, headache and vomiting can be mistaken for signs of many other diseases. But dengue also produces intense muscle and joint pain, which earned the disease the moniker “breakbone fever,” and may progress to leaky blood vessels and death if left untreated.

“Back in the day, there was a lot of focus in the wealthier area, so the center of the town, and so we spread that out,” Igor Normando, Belém’s mayor, said in an interview.

Because of these efforts, he said, mosquito-borne diseases in the city dropped by 70 percent last season.

“The success of this program was a result of the fact that we didn’t just focus on one specific thing,” Mr. Normando said. “We didn’t only focus on education and only rubbish collection and only this or that.”

A core part of Belém’s strategy is its community outreach. Of the city’s more than 1,000 workers in the health department, about a third are focused on limiting mosquito populations. (By contrast, Bay County, Fla., a coastal area of comparable size, has 15 full-time employees in its mosquito control division.)

Many of Belém’s so-called vector control agents go door to door, reminding residents about ways to keep their premises insect-free, keeping water containers covered and mopping up wet spots after the day’s inevitable rainfall. The houses that have the larvicide dissemination units get a monthly visit to replenish supplies and to ensure that the containers have not been refashioned to pot plants or to launder clothes.

On a sweltering day last month, workers on door-to-door rounds discovered that one homeowner’s grandson had thrown the container away when cleaning, not realizing its purpose. Another family hid the container behind two bicycles, to prevent their dogs from getting to it.

As a shirtless Mr. Gomes tried to stay cool in the unrelenting heat, Elizabete Reis, the city agent, inspected the bucket in his veranda for mosquito larvae — there were none — then dumped the water and refilled it. She then added a fresh mesh strip coated with the larvicide, which sticks to female mosquitoes as they land on the strip to lay eggs.

Mr. Gomes said he was “fascinated” to hear that Belém was ahead of many American cities in adopting this approach. “We imagine that this would be something that you would already have, and we always expect these solutions to be coming from the U.S., not for us to be exporting them,” he said.

Most cities in the United States still rely on aerial or truck spraying to control mosquitoes, dispatching the trucks after dusk and warning citizens to stay indoors. The pesticides can cause dizziness, nausea and skin irritation in some people, trigger seizures in some pets and wipe out beneficial insects like bees and butterflies. Brazil, too, initially relied heavily on spraying, but by the early 2000s, the mosquitoes had begun to show signs of resistance to the chemicals. Cities like Belém now resort to fogging — which produces a fine mist rather than the big droplets from sprays — only during outbreaks.

“We cannot just ban the use of insecticides, but we need to use them in a more rational way,” said Dr. Moreira of Wolbito do Brasil. Ideally, insecticides would become part of a larger strategy, to be used mainly during outbreaks, he said, “so that’s what Brazil is doing.”

In 2016, amid widespread insecticide resistance, Brazil’s health ministry convened experts to brainstorm new solutions, including breeding mosquitoes containing Wolbachia bacteria. Wolbachia is an environmentally harmless solution, naturally present in about half of all insects. The technological marvel here was in introducing the bacteria into Aedes aegypti.

The approach is now part of the country’s mosquito-control strategy in 16 cities, but the government plans to expand that number to nearly 80 by the end of next year, Dr. Moreira said.

Belém is not yet on the list to release Wolbachia mosquitoes; it may do so after reducing the numbers with other methods first. But for some residents, the city’s strategy of distributing larvicide units has already brought back unexpected magic.

Filipe Borges, 63, recalled that when Belém sent trucks to fumigate his neighborhood decades ago, the electric blue Amazonian butterflies of his childhood disappeared. But now, he said, there are noticeably fewer mosquitoes in his yard, and yet “the butterflies are back.”

item.title: Early-Onset El Niño
item.description:
About 1,000 miles south of Hawaii, the first signs of El Niño have come to Kiribati, an island nation in the central Pacific Ocean.

Alyssa Atwood, an associate professor in the Earth, ocean and atmospheric science department at Florida State University, is there now, deploying sensors to monitor ocean heat and salinity, and to track the bleaching of the area’s magnificent coral reefs.

Already, around Christmas Island, one of this nation’s 33 atolls and islands, the ocean surface temperature is 2 degrees Celsius, or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, warmer than usual for this time of year, compared with the previous 30 years. And as much as 10 percent of the corals appeared bleached in a series of dives over the past few days, Atwood said.

Bleaching occurs when corals become so stressed that they lose the symbiotic algae they need to survive. Bleached corals can recover, but if the surrounding water stays too hot for too long, they die.

“We expect this to get worse and worse and worse until the end of this year,” she said. “This is just the tip of the iceberg.”

That’s because the El Niño event that’s underway is expected to be one of the strongest ever recorded, and it has not yet peaked.

El Niño is a naturally occurring surge of heat in the Pacific Ocean that usually reaches maximum intensity between December and February. It happens every two to seven years, and it typically spikes global temperatures and scrambles weather patterns around the world.

This year’s event is already strong and having big effects, nudging up global temperatures and causing dry spells and crop failures on multiple continents, my colleagues Raymond Zhong and Chico Harlan wrote in an article this week.

While scientists expect this to be a very strong El Niño, it’s still not entirely clear whether man-made global warming is intensifying the phenomenon.

The El Niños of the past few decades have been comparably strong, Ray and Chico wrote. But the variables that combine to create an El Niño are complex, and some experts argue that the recent trend could just be a random signal.

What is clear is that El Niño’s burst of heat, boosted by climate change or not, is arriving at a moment when global temperatures are already at record highs.

As Eric Niiler wrote in a separate article this year, the past 11 years have been the hottest since record-keeping began. Last year was either the second or third hottest on record, depending on which record is used, he reported, with global average temperatures 1.43 degrees Celsius higher than preindustrial levels. The year 2024 was the hottest, at 1.55 degrees Celsius above the preindustrial average.

All that heat has led to more intense storms, floods, fires and droughts. All of which could become even more intense in the months ahead.

El Niño will magnify those conditions in some regions and could lift global temperatures to record levels next year, as the heat from the Pacific spreads around the world, Ray and Chico wrote.

Atwood said she hoped the data she was gathering in Kiribati could help scientists understand how man-made global warming is affecting El Niños.

“We don’t know what the human fingerprint is on these systems, which is why we have to be out here actually measuring these things in real time, documenting them as much as possible,” she said. “Because these things are happening now on top of background warming in the climate system.”

In Kiribati, El Niño appears to be taking a toll already. Christmas Island, usually very dry this time of year, has been battered by heavy rainfall in recent weeks. During the last very strong El Niño, from 2015 to 2016, heavy rains in the country led to an uptick in mosquito-borne illnesses, including dengue fever and chikungunya virus.

And back then, more than 90 percent of the coral reef around Christmas Island was bleached. The good news, Atwood said, is that much of that coral has recovered over the past decade.

In Panama, normally one of the wettest countries on Earth, some areas haven’t had a major storm since early May. Ethiopia’s fertile highlands are enduring one of their driest summer stretches in four decades. And India had its fifth-driest June since the country’s modern rain records began in 1901.

“It affects weather all around the globe,” Atwood said. “And the bigger the event, the more pronounced those effects get.”

In the coming months, we’ll bring you regular updates about how this event is reshaping the globe and what the science tells us about the climate connection. So stay tuned.

item.title: Electric Thrills
item.description:
It’s Friday, and as promised I have something fun for you: My colleague Chico Harlan, our global climate correspondent, is taking you on a high-adrenaline motorcycle ride through Lahore. And not just on any motorcycle. The bike he rode was electric — as are an increasing number of motorcycles on the streets of Pakistan.

Thrills aside, Chico’s reporting shows something intriguing: The war in Iran has sped up the clean energy transition. In the countries most vulnerable to higher gasoline prices, like Pakistan, the most common vehicles tend to have two wheels, not four. In those countries, the electric motorcycle era has arrived. Hang on tight!

By Chico Harlan

I went to Pakistan last month to learn about the country’s electric motorcycle boom.

Electric motorcycles scarcely existed in Pakistan three years ago, but now sales are surging. The switch signals how quickly, and perhaps permanently, people in developing countries are pivoting away from fossil fuels as the war in Iran keeps oil prices high.

I visited showrooms and an assembly plant and interviewed company founders and would-be buyers. As the trip neared its end, I figured I’d learned just about everything I needed to know.

Except what it feels like to actually ride one.

“Do you want take it out for a drive?” Abdul Rafay, the owner of a new Vlektra electric motorcycle, asked me after we finished an interview.

I looked out at the city of 14 million, as motorbikes pinballed around rickshaws and four-wheelers, and muttered something about journalists not making themselves a part of the story.

But OK, I’d accept a ride. I borrowed a helmet and climbed on the back of Rafay’s bike, just one among the hundreds of thousands of newish, gasoline-free vehicles humming along across Pakistan.

E-bikes and war

Electric motorcycles, it turns out, are a good indicator of the changes driven by the war in Iran. That’s because in poorer countries, where people are most vulnerable to energy-price shocks, two-wheelers are far more common than cars.

Electric vehicles typically cost more to buy than gasoline-powered versions. But rising gasoline prices have given electrics a big advantage: It’s much cheaper to charge a battery than to fill up a fuel tank.

In Vietnam, where the streets teem with motorcycles, the biggest domestic producer, VinFast, has reported soaring sales. In Kenya, about 25 to 35 percent of new motorcycle sales are electric, said Gagan Gupta, the founder of Spiro, the largest electric vehicle company operating in Africa. He said the war’s energy shock had helped “multiply everything by two times.”

People in the industry increasingly talk up the idea that future generations will never operate gasoline-powered vehicles. “The demand is effectively open-ended,” said Josh Whale, the founder of Ampersand, an electric motorcycle company that operates in Kenya and Rwanda.

In Pakistan, motorbikes make up about 80 percent of vehicles on the road and are often the most valuable thing a person owns. The new proliferation of electric motorcycles comes from a mix of homegrown ingenuity and China’s manufacturing prowess.

Some Pakistani companies use chassis and tires manufactured domestically, and batteries and motors from China. But other companies depend on China almost entirely. They import ready-to-assemble bikes that need little more than a logo. Pakistan, aiming to clear up its polluted skies, imposes duties of only 1 percent on such imports.

Sales of electric two-wheelers rose 173 percent during the first half of the year in Pakistan, according to a market data firm, thanks to a government subsidy program and the increase in oil prices that came with the U.S. war with Iran.

“Trump is the biggest salesman — salesman of the year,” said Muhammad Salman, managing director of Yadea Pakistan, the national distributor of Yadea bikes, one of the major brands in China.

‘You got scared, didn’t you?’

On the bike, I hung on tight as Rafay, 24, merged into a roundabout. We were in a relatively upscale part of the city, with painted lane markers and smooth roads. But drivers in Pakistan, I think it can be said, have a strong stomach for adventure.

Rafay clearly wanted to show off his new bike’s power. So he seized on a small opening and accelerated past a rickshaw. He zipped toward two orange vehicles, two or three feet apart. As Rafay darted toward them, a gap opened just large enough to let us through.

The video I was taking with my iPhone doesn’t convey my visceral certainty that one of those orange vehicles was going to clip my knee.

I’d clenched my legs hard enough that Rafay could feel it.

“You got scared, didn’t you?” he asked, looking back.

“Yes,” I said, heart racing a bit, but happy.

Rafay, a gearhead, said he’d loved his previous motorcycle, a Honda CD 70, Pakistan’s most popular gas model. He’d driven it more than 60 kilometers each day to and from his job as a software engineer. But then gasoline costs soared and he started thinking about the math.

“If I can save a few rupees,” he said, “I’ll do it.”

After my ride with Rafay, I thanked him for driving so capably and handed back the helmet.

Then, before the next rains came, I returned to the gas-powered Toyota car I’d been using for the week. It was a vehicle that never made me clench my knees.

Read the full story.

Europe sweltered in the fifth intense heat wave since May, with some temperatures soaring above 40 degrees Celsius. Some people in England are wondering what happened to their cool summers.

Vladimir Putin angered Japan with his first visit to islands the Soviet Union seized at the end of World War II.

Russian strikes on Ukrainian grain ships are once again threatening global food supplies.

An Australian jury found a former Catholic bishop guilty of sexually abusing two young Indigenous men in 2008.

The Israeli military evicted about a dozen settlers who had besieged two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes. Hours later, some of the settlers returned.

Social media tributes to Zhu Rongji, the former Chinese premier, yearned for a more hopeful era when the country was opening to the world.

My colleague Apoorva Mandavilli visited a factory in Brazil where scientists are producing mosquitoes that fight tropical diseases like dengue. Watch the video.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about gadgets that keep you cool.

Although curling is decidedly a winter sport, a synthetic rink was set up in Rome in June. The surface is high-density plastic instead of ice. The stones weigh about a tenth of the regulation weight, and players use brooms to retrieve the stones rather than control their path. The goal? Get Romans to come out and play, despite the blistering heat.

Thousands of software developers across Africa have turned to Chinese A.I. models in the past year. My colleagues interviewed some of them to find out why.

Many developers said they wanted something that worked well on limited resources. They preferred Chinese systems, which anyone can download and modify without payment or approval. “Why use an expensive Ferrari to do the school run when a Toyota hatchback can do the same?” one Nairobi entrepreneur said. Read more about China’s A.I. surge in Africa.

In Bali, fireflies are revered as sacred messengers, a connection between living communities and their ancestors. But they’re disappearing across the Indonesian island because of climate change and environmental threats.

I Wayan Wardika has embarked on a quest to restore what he calls “the magic of fireflies.” He has started Indonesia’s first firefly conservation facility, where he breeds and raises them in terrariums named “honeymoon suites.” Read more and see the lab.

This version of the classic Southern lane cake takes all of fruitcake’s best elements — bourbon-soaked dried fruit, toasty pecans and shredded coconut — and weaves them into a rich, custardy filling set between three layers of tender vanilla cake. It’s a dessert and a nightcap, rolled into one.

Which island is this?

Naoshima, Japan

Sicily, Italy

Spitsbergen, Norway

Don Det, Laos

One of the things I love most about summer is that life slows down a little and I get to carve out time to read the books and listen to the podcasts that have piled up, literally and figuratively.

I’ll share some of my highlights in case you still have a bit of vacation time left.

My favorite nonfiction book this summer was “Peak Human” by Johan Norberg, a Swedish historian who tells the story of seven golden ages of humanity — including ancient Athens, the Abbasid Caliphate, the Song dynasty and the modern West. He explores what allowed humans to flourish in each of those periods and what we can learn from them today. (Spoiler alert: All of them were open to ideas and trade.)

My favorite novel was “The Safekeep” by Yael van der Wouden. I had to get used to the writing, which is sparse and self-conscious, and initially a little annoying, partly to channel the main character — a complicated, intensely controlling and, yes, annoying, woman. But two plot twists later, the book is kind of a masterpiece. The backdrop is post-Holocaust Europe. I won’t say more.

My favorite podcast was “The Gaza Chef,” a five-part documentary by Yassin Musharbash, an investigative journalist at the German weekly Die Zeit. It’s a compelling and balanced investigation into the death of Mahmud Almadhoun, who ran a soup kitchen in the northern Gaza Strip and was killed by an Israeli drone two years ago. I couldn’t say it better than the tagline of the podcast: “The question of why he had to die leads deep into the worrisome future of warfare.”

Musharbash once worked as a fixer for John le Carré and has written a series of novels himself. He knows how to tell a good story!

And finally, my favorite feel-good holiday song this year: “Love Chain” by Candi Staton, a summer classic. Enjoy!

Have a great weekend! — Katrin
